slides.title: Start with the symptoms that prompted the culture
slides.section: Start with the symptoms that prompted the culture
paragraphs: An 82-year-old is admitted with confusion after poor intake and a medication change. Temperature and blood pressure are normal. There is no dysuria, new urgency, suprapubic pain, or flank pain. Urine testing shows pyuria and more than 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli.
Discuss before reading on. What establishes a urinary infection here? What other explanations for delirium need evaluation?
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Start with the symptoms that prompted the culture An 82-year-old is admitted with confusion after poor intake and a medication change. Temperature and blood pressure are normal. There is no dysuria, new urgency, suprapubic pain, or flank pain. Urine testing shows pyuria and more than 100,000 CFU/mL of E. coli. Discuss before reading on. What establishes a urinary infection here? What other explanations for delirium need evaluation? Asymptomatic bacteriuria means bacteria in urine without an attributable urinary infection syndrome. Pyuria can accompany colonization. Neither the organism name nor its resistance pattern establishes a need for antibiotics. [1] [2]

slides.title: Decide whether urine testing can answer a clinical question
slides.section: Decide whether urine testing can answer a clinical question
rows: Clinical finding
Approach
New dysuria, frequency, urgency, or suprapubic pain
Assess for symptomatic lower UTI and competing causes. Culture when it will guide management.
Fever with flank pain, rigors, or otherwise unexplained systemic illness
Evaluate for systemic UTI and alternative sources; obtain a culture when UTI is plausible.
Delirium or a fall without urinary symptoms, fever, or instability
Assess other causes and observe. Bacteriuria alone does not establish the cause.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Decide whether urine testing can answer a clinical question A positive result is useful only in the clinical context. Clinical finding Approach New dysuria, frequency, urgency, or suprapubic pain Assess for symptomatic lower UTI and competing causes. Culture when it will guide management. Fever with flank pain, rigors, or otherwise unexplained systemic illness Evaluate for systemic UTI and alternative sources; obtain a culture when UTI is plausible. Delirium or a fall without urinary symptoms, fever, or instability Assess other causes and observe. Bacteriuria alone does not establish the cause. Cloudy urine, odor, or pyuria alone Do not use these findings alone to trigger treatment. Avoid collecting a culture solely to explain them. In a patient unable to report symptoms, obtain collateral history, examine for localizing findings, and reassess the trajectory. Inability to give a history is not proof that bacteriuria is symptomatic. [1] [2] [3]

slides.title: Treat established exceptions rather than every positive culture
slides.section: Treat established exceptions rather than every positive culture
rows: Pregnancy
Management of bacteriuria without symptoms
Screen with a urine culture and treat confirmed ASB using a pregnancy-appropriate, susceptibility-directed regimen.
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Treat established exceptions rather than every positive culture The type of procedure matters; not every urologic encounter breaches mucosa. Situation Management of bacteriuria without symptoms Pregnancy Screen with a urine culture and treat confirmed ASB using a pregnancy-appropriate, susceptibility-directed regimen. Endoscopic urologic procedure with expected mucosal trauma Culture beforehand and provide targeted peri-procedural therapy. IDSA suggests 1 or 2 doses beginning 30-60 minutes before the procedure. Older adults, diabetes, chronic catheters, or elective joint arthroplasty Do not routinely screen for or treat ASB. Standard surgical prophylaxis is a separate decision. Pregnancy treatment and follow-up should follow the obstetric pathway. Do not extrapolate the short peri-procedural regimen to pregnancy. [1] [2] [4]

slides.title: A urinary catheter makes colonization more likely
slides.section: A urinary catheter makes colonization more likely
paragraphs: Catheter biofilm makes persistent or recurrent bacteriuria common. Antibiotics given to sterilize asymptomatic urine expose patients to adverse effects, C. difficile, and resistance without treating a symptomatic infection. Review whether the catheter is still needed. [3]

When symptomatic infection is suspected, obtain a properly collected sample. Use the sampling port with aseptic technique, not the drainage bag. Catheter removal or replacement is a separate source-control decision; follow the CAUTI pathway when infection is suspected. [5]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
A urinary catheter makes colonization more likely Catheter biofilm makes persistent or recurrent bacteriuria common. Antibiotics given to sterilize asymptomatic urine expose patients to adverse effects, C. difficile, and resistance without treating a symptomatic infection. Review whether the catheter is still needed. [3] When symptomatic infection is suspected, obtain a properly collected sample. Use the sampling port with aseptic technique, not the drainage bag. Catheter removal or replacement is a separate source-control decision; follow the CAUTI pathway when infection is suspected. [5] A catheter plus a positive culture is not, by itself, a catheter-associated UTI. [3]

slides.title: Return to the patient and write the clinical assessment
slides.section: Return to the patient and write the clinical assessment
paragraphs: For the opening case, the available findings support ASB. Do not start or continue antibiotics solely for the urine result. Evaluate the delirium, correct identified contributors, and follow the examination and vital signs. [1]
If fever, hypotension, or another sign of serious infection develops, reassess promptly for urinary and nonurinary sources. The initial ASB assessment does not exclude a later infection. [1]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Return to the patient and write the clinical assessment For the opening case, the available findings support ASB. Do not start or continue antibiotics solely for the urine result. Evaluate the delirium, correct identified contributors, and follow the examination and vital signs. [1] If fever, hypotension, or another sign of serious infection develops, reassess promptly for urinary and nonurinary sources. The initial ASB assessment does not exclude a later infection. [1] Example documentation. "Bacteriuria without localizing urinary symptoms or systemic signs of infection. No antibiotic indication from the urine result. Evaluating other causes of delirium and monitoring for clinical change." In a 46-hospital observational cohort of 2,733 patients with ASB, treatment was not associated with better measured clinical outcomes and was associated with a longer stay after urine testing. This was an association, not proof that antibiotics caused the additional hospital days. [6]

slides.title: Recognize where the evidence is incomplete
slides.section: Recognize where the evidence is incomplete
paragraphs: IDSA recommends against screening or treatment more than 1 month after kidney transplantation. The first month after kidney transplantation and high-risk neutropenia remain knowledge gaps in that guideline; involve the relevant specialty rather than extrapolating the routine ward rule. [1]
In spinal cord injury, new spasticity, autonomic dysreflexia, or new incontinence may contribute to a UTI assessment. Establish a change from baseline and look for other causes. [2]
slides.notes:
Complete source section:
Recognize where the evidence is incomplete IDSA recommends against screening or treatment more than 1 month after kidney transplantation. The first month after kidney transplantation and high-risk neutropenia remain knowledge gaps in that guideline; involve the relevant specialty rather than extrapolating the routine ward rule. [1] In spinal cord injury, new spasticity, autonomic dysreflexia, or new incontinence may contribute to a UTI assessment. Establish a change from baseline and look for other causes. [2] The formal midstream definition uses at least 10 5 CFU/mL, with persistence confirmed in two specimens in women and one in men. That definition is not a reason to repeat an unnecessary culture. Symptomatic UTI can occur with lower counts. [2] Discussion variation. An asymptomatic patient is scheduled for ureteroscopy with lithotripsy. Explain why the procedural plan changes management while a planned knee replacement does not. [1] [2]
